name: Fatima Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and a junior operator feeding ceramic tiles through a glaze line before the kiln. I finished secondary school and still ask the lead to check my spray setting. I like seeing an even colour after firing; a clogged nozzle can spoil a whole row before I notice.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home life like, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner counts stock at a food warehouse. We have two school-age children, nine and thirteen, and a mortgage. I earn typical factory pay, we have about three months of expenses saved, and there are some similar plants nearby. I never use AI tools; I keep the spray checks on a paper card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the tile line a neater order sheet is fine, but it won't show whether a glazed tile stuck to the kiln roller. A person still has to stop the belt and inspect the surface.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two wages cover the mortgage and children, and we have roughly three months of expenses saved. I earn the usual operator rate, and there are some other factories nearby. A small AI change leaves our pay secure for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep feeding tiles onto the glaze line and call the lead when the spray pattern goes patchy. I want another month of supervised changeovers so I can set the nozzle without wasting a batch. I won't use an AI tool myself; my paper checks are clear enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about this picture. I'd rather get good at the machine in front of me than chase a tool the office says is clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you catch before firing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week I caught a row of dull tiles where the spray nozzle had clogged. A clogged glaze nozzle can spoil a whole row of tiles before firing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you plan household money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner counts stock at a food warehouse and our children are nine and thirteen. We compare pay with the mortgage on Sundays; I would keep that habit even if the office gets a quicker list.

say: **AI order sheets** may improve while people still check wet tile glaze and kiln rollers.
The **tile crew** should stop a patchy batch before firing.
think: Our two **regular wages** and three-month reserve cover current bills.
Some **nearby factories** provide options if the tile plant changes later.
do: **Keep** feeding tiles and inspecting glaze before the kiln.
**Practice** nozzle changeovers with the lead during paid shifts.
feel: **Calm** while tile work and household wages continue.
S0.quote: A clogged glaze nozzle can spoil a whole row of tiles before firing.
fieldNote: Fatima is **resistant to AI** and prefers supervised physical learning to a new screen.
The **moderate reserve** and two current wages support calm in a mild outcome.

steps.text: Keep feeding and checking glazed tiles before kiln firing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our union branch that buying and warehouse counts could change before robots run the tile belt. Paid people should check the stock numbers, and anyone moved off that work needs real notice and training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner counts pallets at a warehouse, so AI stock checking could shorten that job before the glaze line changes. Three months saved would carry us for a while, but the mortgage needs two wages for longer. I am not eager to learn a new AI screen myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the union steward to take warehouse-hour and tile-crew questions to the joint meeting. My partner will request a written roster plan from the warehouse. I'll keep the paid tile shifts and practise the mechanical nozzle changeover I already need for my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household wage, though my own tile hours look steady in the short run. I don't want a stock report to arrive before the news that a shift has gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a written warehouse plan show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The warehouse should say which pallet counts are moving to software and how many paid counting hours remain. A vague promise of other work won't cover our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you practise on the tile line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd record what went wrong in the last three glaze runs and ask the lead for paid time to practise the nozzle setting. That is ordinary machine skill, not learning AI.

say: **Stock counting** may change before hands-on tile glazing does.
The **union meeting** should seek clear paid-hour plans and real training.
think: My partner's **warehouse wage** could shrink under faster stock checking.
Three months of **savings** help briefly, but the mortgage needs longer income.
do: **Raise** household hour concerns through the joint union meeting.
**Request** a written warehouse roster plan with my partner.
**Continue** paid tile shifts and learn the mechanical nozzle setting.
feel: **Anxious** about a realistic household wage reduction.
S1.quote: A vague promise of other work won't cover our mortgage.
fieldNote: Her **own tile role** stays physical in slower disruption, while her partner’s stock-counting job is directly exposed.
She seeks **collective notice** and familiar mechanical practice without claiming AI learning.

steps.text: Raise warehouse and tile paid-hour questions through union steward
Keep paid tile shifts and practise mechanical nozzle setting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI by 2028 could run warehouse stock counts, and capable robots around 2031 could load and glaze tiles. I'd tell the union we need wage protection before both jobs are reduced, not a course flyer handed out afterward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my partner's warehouse counting hours to fall sharply by 2028 and my junior glaze work to be at risk when robots arrive. Three months of savings cannot cover a long two-wage gap. I've been waking before dawn doing the mortgage arithmetic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week we'll ask both employers for written staffing plans. If either wage is cut, I'll apply to posted local production jobs with regular pay and hours enough for the mortgage and school costs. If the tile plant offers a funded, paid-time practical course on guarding and maintaining the robot glaze line, I'll enrol only with a real supervised place; I'll keep my current wage while it is offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because the household could lose a large share of income before we replace it. I can ask for plans, but a plan won't pay the next mortgage bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must practical training teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the instructor to isolate the glaze sprayer, prove the belt cannot restart and let me set a nozzle with a lead beside me. A video would not make me safe near a moving conveyor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge a local posting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The posting must be reachable after school drop-off and show base pay, not just possible overtime. I would compare it with our monthly mortgage, food and travel before applying.

say: **2028 thinking AI** may cut warehouse counting before robots glaze tiles around 2031.
The union needs **written staffing plans** and income protection across both workplaces.
think: A sharp **warehouse wage cut** and later junior tile loss threaten our mortgage.
Three months of **savings** cannot cover a long two-wage gap.
do: **Ask** both employers for written hour plans this week.
**Apply** to posted local production work if wages fall and base pay covers bills.
**Enrol** in practical glaze-robot course if funded paid supervised place offered.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major income loss and broken sleep.
S2.quote: A video would not make me safe near a moving conveyor.
fieldNote: The **fast timing** exposes warehouse pay first and physical tile work around 2031.
She separates **training** from an actual local application, each with funding or pay conditions.

steps.text: Ask both warehouse and tile employers for written staffing plans
Apply if wages cut to posted local production role reachable after school drop-off with bill-covering hours/pay
Enrol in glaze-robot course if funded paid supervised safe place offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If thinking AI reaches warehouse counts in 2031 and robots handle tile glazing around 2034, I'd tell the union five years gives us time to demand real course places. We should not wait for the first lost pallet shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when warehouse work changes and 51 when physical robots reach my tile line. Our children will still need money and we may still owe on the mortgage. The three-month reserve gives us a starting point, not five years of income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep paid tile shifts and add new savings from each full pay month after the mortgage and food. If the plant offers a recognized glaze-line maintenance course with fees, paid release and guarded hands-on practice, I'll enrol next year. If qualified and either wage later falls, I'll apply to posted local maintenance roles only when safe duties, regular hours and base pay meet our household needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about future wages, but the longer warning gives me time to practise on a stopped machine. I would take the new course if it is paid and clearly leads to a real job option.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the first practical lesson include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first lesson should be an isolated spray head and a tile with a deliberately thin glaze. I need to see how the alarm compares with the actual surface.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide whether to move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A course certificate alone is not a wage. I'd check the posted job's hourly rate and rota before making any move from the current paid tile line.

say: **2031 thinking AI** changes stock counts before robots glaze tiles around 2034.
The union should secure **real paid course places** before shifts fall.
think: At **51**, I may still need tile or maintenance pay.
A **three-month reserve** helps training decisions but cannot replace a wage for years.
do: **Keep** paid tile work and add new savings after full months.
**Enrol** in funded recognized maintenance training if paid guarded place offered.
**Apply** to posted local maintenance after qualifying if wage falls and pay suffices.
feel: **Anxious** about household income, with more time to gain safe skills.
S3.quote: A course certificate alone is not a wage.
fieldNote: She accepts **practical retraining** under concrete fee, paid-time and safety conditions despite personal caution.
The subsequent **job application** depends on qualification, wage loss and posted safe local pay.

steps.text: Save new money from full paid tile months after bills
Enrol in recognized course if funded paid guarded place offered
Apply for posted safe local maintenance if qualified, wage cut, pay sufficient

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2036 could change warehouse counting, and capable robots around 2039 could handle the glaze line. I'd tell the union we have time to bargain for paid training and notice before either roster is cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 at the AI date and 56 when robots can glaze tiles. We may have less mortgage left, but I won't assume it is gone. Our three-month reserve and two wages make the next few years feel secure; the later handover still sits in my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the tile work and save a fresh portion of each full wage if bills allow. I'll ask the union training committee to seek recognized guarded glaze-line lessons on paid time. If a real funded place is offered, I'll take it; if later paid hours fall, I'll apply to posted qualified local roles with safe duties and enough base pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the distant handover, while today's work and income look stable. A decade lets me learn slowly without giving up the current wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you practise first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd first practise stopping the glaze belt and checking a fired tile against a hand sample. I would need an instructor and a guarded line, not an online slide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you review the household plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would review the mortgage balance each year and count only savings actually added from pay. If the warehouse or tile roster shrinks, a local posted wage would have to cover the children and the bills.

say: **2036 thinking AI** changes warehouse counts before robots glaze tiles around 2039.
The union should bargain for **paid guarded instruction** and roster notice.
think: At **56**, I may still need a wage even if the mortgage shrinks.
Current **two wages** and three months saved make near-term income secure.
do: **Keep** tile shifts and add new savings from full pay.
**Attend** recognised guarded glaze-line training only if an actual funded paid place is offered.
**Apply** for posted qualified local work if later hours fall and pay suffices.
feel: **Uneasy** about distant change with current wages intact.
S4.quote: A decade lets me learn slowly without giving up the current wage.
fieldNote: She distinguishes **future robot timing** from her secure current wages and conditional mortgage balance.
Offered **paid training** and any later local application retain safety, qualification and pay conditions.

steps.text: Save new money from full tile wages when bills allow
Seek funded paid guarded lessons through union committee
Attend recognized glaze course if funded paid safe place offered

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case worries me most. My partner's warehouse counting hours could be cut before capable glaze-line robots reach my work around 2031. Written staffing plans, funded paid practical training and a real local job with enough pay would help us keep the mortgage covered.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets to stop the kiln line when the tiles come through with thin glaze. A neat stock count cannot put glaze back on a fired tile.

headlineQuote: A neat stock count cannot put glaze back on a fired tile.
portrait: **Fatima**, 43, is a junior ceramic-tile glaze operator with secondary school education and typical factory pay.
She and her warehouse-worker partner support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage with three months saved.
She **never uses AI** and prefers familiar guarded practical training over a new screen.
She starts **calm** with two wages, but fast warehouse and tile automation make her anxious or alarmed.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut warehouse counting pay before robots threaten her junior glaze work around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Written staffing plans**, funded paid guarded instruction and a posted safe local job at enough pay would help.
